items.title: Digital
items.tagline: Time as numbers. From the red glow of 1970s LED to the near-indestructible LCDs that live on millions of wrists.

subcategories.name: LCD
subcategories.text: Liquid-crystal displays that are always on and sip power. Batteries can last 7 to 10 years.

subcategories.name: LED
subcategories.text: The original 1970s digital watch. You pressed a button to light up red digits, and batteries drained quickly.

subcategories.name: Ana-digi
subcategories.text: Analog hands combined with a digital display, such as many G-Shock and Pro Trek models.

subcategories.name: Rugged / tool digital
subcategories.text: Shock-resistant, water-resistant and packed with functions such as altimeters, compasses and tide graphs.

subcategories.name: Data and calculator watches
subcategories.text: 1980s icons with calculators, databanks and even TV remotes built in.

items.body:
In the early 1970s the digital watch was the height of luxury: the first Pulsar cost more than a car. Within a decade, LCD technology had made digital watches the cheapest timekeepers ever made.

## Why digital matters to collectors

Digital watches are design and technology history you can actually wear. The **Casio F-91W**, the **G-Shock**, the **Seiko** "James Bond" LCD watches and the **Hamilton Pulsar** are all collectible, and many cost very little.

## Buying tips

- Check the **module number** on the caseback. It tells you exactly which functions the watch has.
- Look for **solar** and **radio-controlled** versions if you never want to set or change a battery.
- For tough use, the **G-Shock** standard of shock resistance is the benchmark.

items.title: Exotic
items.tagline: Tuning forks, jumping hours, wandering numerals and pure concept pieces. The beautifully strange side of horology.

subcategories.name: Tuning fork
subcategories.text: The Bulova Accutron (1960) used a tuning fork vibrating at 360 Hz. It hums instead of ticking.

subcategories.name: Jump hour
subcategories.text: The hour appears as a numeral in a window and jumps instantly on the hour, often with a separate minute display.

subcategories.name: Wandering hour
subcategories.text: Hour numerals travel along an arc, pointing to the minutes as they go. A 17th-century idea revived by modern makers.

subcategories.name: Mechanical digital
subcategories.text: Watches that show time as numbers using mechanical discs, like the A. Lange & Söhne Zeitwerk.

subcategories.name: Concept and art pieces
subcategories.text: Independents such as MB&F, Urwerk and HYT reinvent how a watch can display time.

facts.v: Service access matters, so check it first

items.body:
Exotic watches are where horology becomes art. Some are historical dead ends, like the tuning-fork watch overtaken by quartz, and some are modern experiments in how we read time.

## Collecting exotics

- **Know who can service it.** Tuning-fork and early electronic watches need specialists.
- **Documentation matters even more** for independents and low-production pieces.
- **Wear before you buy.** Unusual displays can be thrilling or frustrating in daily life.

items.title: Hybrid
items.tagline: Where mechanics meet electronics. Watches that borrow the best of both worlds.

subcategories.name: Spring Drive
subcategories.text: Seiko and Grand Seiko's technology. A mainspring powers the watch, and a quartz-regulated electromagnetic brake controls its speed. The seconds hand glides perfectly smoothly.

subcategories.name: Hybrid smartwatch
subcategories.text: A traditional analog watch face with hidden sensors for steps, sleep and notifications, and batteries that last weeks or months.

subcategories.name: Mecaquartz
subcategories.text: A quartz timekeeping movement with a mechanical chronograph module, giving a crisp mechanical pusher feel.

subcategories.name: Auto-quartz
subcategories.text: Quartz regulation charged by a rotor (Seiko Kinetic and similar), sometimes also counted as quartz.

facts.v: People who want character and convenience

items.body:
Hybrid watches resist easy classification, and that is exactly what makes them fascinating.

## Spring Drive in one paragraph

The mainspring unwinds through a normal gear train, but instead of an escapement, the final wheel, the **glide wheel**, spins continuously. As it spins it generates a small current that powers a quartz crystal and an integrated circuit. The circuit compares the glide wheel's speed with the crystal and applies a precise **electromagnetic brake**. There is no tick, just a seconds hand that flows like time itself.

## Hybrid smartwatches

Brands such as Withings and Garmin hide activity tracking inside classic-looking cases. They suit people who want health data without a glowing screen.

items.title: Mechanical
items.tagline: Springs, gears and a beating heart. No battery, just energy stored in a coiled spring and released one tick at a time.

subcategories.name: Manual-wind
subcategories.text: Wound by turning the crown, usually every day or two. Thinner and more intimate, with no rotor blocking the view of the movement.

subcategories.name: Automatic (central rotor)
subcategories.text: A weighted rotor spins with your wrist movements and winds the mainspring. The most common type of mechanical watch today.

subcategories.name: Micro-rotor
subcategories.text: A small rotor set into the movement itself, which allows thin automatic watches with an unobstructed view of the finishing.

subcategories.name: Peripheral rotor
subcategories.text: A weighted ring that runs around the edge of the movement, leaving the whole calibre visible.

items.body:
A mechanical watch is a small machine that stores energy in a **mainspring** and lets it out in perfectly measured steps. The energy flows through the **gear train** to the **escapement**, which gives regular impulses to the **balance wheel**. The balance and its hairspring swing back and forth several times a second, and every swing lets the gear train advance a tiny bit. That is the tick you hear.

## Why people still love them

A quartz watch is more accurate and cheaper. People choose mechanical for the same reasons they choose a fountain pen or a vinyl record: craft, longevity and the sense of owning something alive. A well-made mechanical watch can be serviced and kept running for generations.

## What to look for

- **Movement**: a proven workhorse (ETA, Sellita, Seiko, Miyota) or an in-house calibre
- **Power reserve**: 70–80 hours means the watch survives a weekend off the wrist
- **Hacking and hand-winding**: convenient for setting the time precisely
- **Anti-magnetism**: silicon hairsprings or a soft-iron cage resist everyday magnets

## Start here

Read [How a mechanical movement works](../../learn/automatic/how-a-mechanical-movement-works/), then explore the calibre database.

items.title: Quartz Analog
items.tagline: A sliver of quartz crystal vibrating 32,768 times a second, counted by a chip and turned into the steady step of a seconds hand.

subcategories.name: Standard quartz
subcategories.text: Battery-powered, accurate to around ±15 seconds a month, inexpensive and virtually maintenance-free.

subcategories.name: High-accuracy quartz (HAQ)
subcategories.text: Thermocompensated movements that correct for temperature, accurate to about ±10 seconds a year.

subcategories.name: Solar
subcategories.text: A photovoltaic cell under the dial charges a rechargeable cell. Citizen Eco-Drive and Casio Tough Solar are the best known.

subcategories.name: Kinetic / auto-quartz
subcategories.text: A rotor like an automatic's spins a tiny generator to charge the cell.

subcategories.name: Radio-controlled and GPS
subcategories.text: The watch synchronises itself with atomic clock radio signals or GPS satellites and is effectively always exact.

items.body:
When Seiko sold the first quartz wristwatch on Christmas Day 1969, it began the **quartz crisis**: within fifteen years, cheap and astonishingly accurate quartz watches had devastated the traditional Swiss industry.

## How it works

A battery sends current through a tiny tuning-fork-shaped quartz crystal. Quartz is *piezoelectric*: it vibrates at a precise frequency when electrified. An integrated circuit counts 32,768 vibrations and sends one pulse per second to a stepper motor that moves the hands.

## Why choose quartz

- **Accuracy** that the best mechanical watches cannot match
- **Grab-and-go**: no winding, no setting after a weekend off the wrist
- **Thin and light** cases
- **Cost**: superb quartz watches exist at every price, up to Grand Seiko 9F and beyond

Quartz is not a lesser choice, it is a different one. Many collectors keep at least one excellent quartz piece in the box.

items.title: Smartwatch
items.tagline: A computer that also tells the time. Health sensors, notifications, GPS and payments, all on the wrist.

subcategories.name: Full operating system
subcategories.text: Apple watchOS, Google Wear OS, Samsung, Huawei HarmonyOS. Third-party apps, rich notifications, payments and voice assistants.

subcategories.name: Fitness trackers
subcategories.text: Slimmer devices focused on steps, sleep, heart rate and workouts, with batteries that last a week or more.

subcategories.name: Outdoor and multisport
subcategories.text: Garmin, Coros, Suunto and others. Precise GPS, maps, training load, and batteries measured in weeks.

subcategories.name: Kids and safety
subcategories.text: Location tracking, calling and SOS features for children and older people.

facts.v: Optical heart rate, accelerometer, GPS, SpO₂, ECG, temperature

items.body:
Smartwatches are now the best-selling category of watch in the world by volume. For collectors they raise new questions: **how long will it be supported?**, **which ecosystem am I locked into?** and **what happens to my health data?**

## Choosing a smartwatch

1. **Match your phone.** Apple Watch only works with iPhone; most others work best with Android.
2. **Decide what matters: battery or apps.** Full-OS watches charge daily; outdoor watches can last weeks.
3. **Check sensor accuracy** for the sports you do. Wrist heart rate is weaker for intervals and weightlifting.
4. **Think about longevity.** A mechanical watch lasts generations; a smartwatch typically lasts a few years.

## Smartwatches and traditional watches

Many enthusiasts wear both: a smartwatch for training, a mechanical watch for everything else. Hybrid watches try to combine the two, see the Hybrid section.
